lessons.title: Solar system, stability of orbital motions and satellites
lessons.summary: Tour the structure of our solar system, follow the life cycle of a star from nebula to white dwarf or black hole, and explain how gravity keeps planets and satellites in stable orbits.
objectives: I can describe the structure of the solar system and its place in the Milky Way.
I can explain how a star forms and how fusion balances gravity in a stable main sequence star.
I can describe the life cycle of stars of different masses and explain how heavier elements are made and distributed.
I can explain how gravity provides the force for circular orbital motion and why a change in speed changes the orbit radius (Higher).
I can describe the difference between natural and artificial satellites.

activities.title: Our solar system
activities.content:
## What is in the solar system?

The **solar system** is everything that orbits our star, the **Sun**. Working outwards from the Sun:

- **Eight planets**: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars (small, rocky), then Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (large, gaseous). Planets orbit the Sun in nearly circular paths.
- **Dwarf planets** such as Pluto and Ceres: round bodies that orbit the Sun but have not cleared other objects from their orbits.
- **Moons**: natural satellites that orbit planets. Earth has one; Jupiter has more than ninety.
- **Asteroids**: lumps of rock, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.
- **Comets**: icy objects on very elongated (highly elliptical) orbits, which grow tails when they approach the Sun.

The Sun contains more than 99 % of the mass of the solar system, which is why everything else orbits it.

### Zooming out
The Sun is just one of billions of stars in our **galaxy**, the **Milky Way**. The Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies in the **Universe**.

| Object | What orbits it |
|---|---|
| Sun | planets, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets |
| Planet | moons, artificial satellites |
| Galaxy centre | hundreds of billions of stars including the Sun |

question.text: Put these objects in order of size, starting with the SMALLEST.
question.hint: Moons orbit planets, planets orbit stars, stars are grouped in galaxies.
question.explanation: Moon → planet → star (Sun) → solar system → galaxy → Universe.

activities.title: How a star is born
activities.content:
## From dust to star

Every star begins as a **nebula**: a huge cloud of **dust and gas**, mostly hydrogen, spread thinly across space.

1. **Gravity** pulls the particles of the cloud together. As the cloud collapses it becomes denser and the particles move faster, so the **temperature rises**.
2. The collapsing, warming ball is called a **protostar**. It glows but is not yet a true star.
3. When the core becomes **hot and dense enough**, **nuclear fusion** begins: hydrogen nuclei fuse to form **helium**, releasing enormous amounts of energy. The protostar has become a **main sequence star**.

## Why a main sequence star is stable
Two forces fight inside the star:
- **Gravity** pulls everything inwards, trying to make the star collapse.
- The **energy released by fusion** creates an outward pressure (radiation and hot gas pushing out), trying to make the star expand.

In a main sequence star these are **balanced**, so the star stays the same size and gives out a steady light. This state can last billions of years: the Sun has been on the main sequence for about 4.6 billion years and has roughly 5 billion left.

The Sun's energy, and the energy of every star, comes from **fusion of hydrogen into helium**, not from burning. Nothing is on fire.

question.text: Complete the sentence about main sequence stars.

metadata.blanksText: A main sequence star is stable because the inward force of ___ is balanced by the outward pressure produced by nuclear ___ in its core.

question.hint: One pulls in; the other releases energy that pushes out.
question.explanation: Gravity pulls inwards; the energy from nuclear fusion pushes outwards; the two balance.

activities.title: The life cycle of a star
activities.content:
## What happens when the hydrogen runs out?

Eventually the hydrogen in the core is used up, fusion slows and the balance breaks. What happens next depends on the **mass** of the star.

### Stars about the size of the Sun
1. **Red giant**: the core shrinks and heats up while the outer layers **expand and cool**, so the star becomes huge and red. Helium now fuses into heavier elements such as carbon and oxygen.
2. The outer layers drift away, leaving the hot core as a **white dwarf**. No fusion happens any more; it shines only because it is still hot.
3. Over a very long time it cools and fades to a **black dwarf**.

### Stars much more massive than the Sun
1. **Red super giant**: like a red giant but far larger. Fusion continues, building heavier and heavier elements up to **iron**.
2. When fusion stops the star collapses suddenly and rebounds in a gigantic explosion: a **supernova**. This is the only place elements **heavier than iron** are made.
3. The remaining core becomes either a **neutron star** (incredibly dense, a few kilometres across) or, if the star was very massive, a **black hole** (gravity so strong that not even light escapes).

```
Nebula → Protostar → Main sequence star
                          │
        ┌─────────────────┴─────────────────┐
   Sun-sized                            Much more massive
   Red giant                            Red super giant
   White dwarf                          Supernova
   Black dwarf                     Neutron star / Black hole
```

### Where the elements come from
Fusion in stars makes all the naturally occurring elements up to iron. Supernovae make the heavier ones and **scatter** every element through space. New stars and planets form from this enriched dust, which is why the Earth (and you) contain carbon, oxygen, iron and gold. The presence of these elements in our solar system is evidence that it formed from the remains of earlier stars.

question.text: Put the stages in the life cycle of a star about the same mass as the Sun in the correct order.
question.hint: It starts as a cloud and ends as a cold, dark remnant.
question.explanation: Nebula → protostar → main sequence star → red giant → white dwarf → black dwarf.

question.text: Which TWO statements about stars much more massive than the Sun are correct?
question.hint: Think about the supernova stage and what it leaves behind.
question.explanation: Massive stars become red super giants, explode as supernovae (which create and scatter elements heavier than iron) and leave a neutron star or black hole. They do not become white dwarfs, and they have shorter, not longer, lives because they use fuel faster.

options.text: They explode as a supernova, which produces elements heavier than iron
The remaining core becomes a neutron star or a black hole
They end their lives as white dwarfs
options.feedback: White dwarfs are the remains of Sun-sized stars.

options.text: They stay on the main sequence for longer than the Sun
options.feedback: Massive stars burn their fuel much faster and have shorter lives.

activities.title: Orbits and gravity
activities.content:
## What keeps things in orbit?

Planets orbit the Sun, moons and artificial satellites orbit planets. In every case the force that holds the object in orbit is **gravity**.

### Circular motion (Higher)
An object moving in a circle at a **constant speed** is nevertheless **accelerating**, because its **direction** (and therefore its **velocity**) is constantly changing. Acceleration needs a resultant force, and for an orbit that force is gravity, which acts **towards the centre** of the orbit. The speed stays the same because the force is always at right angles to the motion: it changes direction, not speed.

### Speed and radius (Higher)
For a **stable** orbit at a particular radius there is exactly **one speed** that works:
- Closer orbits need a **higher speed** (gravity is stronger there, so the object must move faster to avoid being pulled in).
- Further orbits need a **lower speed**.

If a satellite's speed **changes**, the radius of its orbit **must change** too. Slow it down and it drops to a lower orbit; speed it up and it climbs to a higher one.

Mercury, closest to the Sun, races round at about 47 km/s; Neptune, far out, crawls at about 5 km/s.

## Satellites
- A **natural satellite** is a moon: a natural object in orbit around a planet.
- An **artificial satellite** is a machine put into orbit by people, used for communication, weather forecasting, GPS, astronomy and spying.

**Geostationary** satellites orbit high above the equator once every 24 hours, so they stay above the same spot on Earth (ideal for TV broadcasting). **Low polar orbit** satellites circle much closer, every 90 minutes or so, passing over the whole surface (ideal for weather and mapping).

activities.title: Worked example: thinking about orbits
activities.content:
**A satellite is in a circular orbit around the Earth. Its speed is constant. Explain why it is accelerating and what provides the force.**

Velocity is a vector. The satellite's **speed** is constant but its **direction** changes continuously as it goes round, so its **velocity** is changing. A changing velocity means an **acceleration**. The acceleration is directed towards the centre of the Earth, and the force that produces it is the **gravitational attraction** between the Earth and the satellite.

**Mission control fires the satellite's thrusters briefly so that it slows down. What happens to its orbit?**

At the original radius, only the original speed gives a stable orbit. At a lower speed, gravity is too strong for that radius and pulls the satellite **inwards**. It settles into a **smaller** orbit closer to the Earth (where, in fact, it ends up moving faster again).

**Two satellites, A and B, orbit the Earth. A is 400 km up and B is 36 000 km up. Which moves faster?**

**A.** The closer satellite experiences stronger gravity and needs the higher speed to stay in orbit. A completes an orbit in about 90 minutes; B takes 24 hours.

question.text: A satellite moves to an orbit with a larger radius. For its orbit to remain stable, its speed must:
question.hint: Gravity is weaker further away, so less speed is needed to balance it.
question.explanation: For a stable orbit, a larger radius requires a lower speed. Gravity is weaker further out, so the satellite needs less speed to keep from falling inwards.

options.feedback: Higher speed is needed for a closer orbit, not a further one.

question.text: True or false: a planet in a circular orbit at constant speed has zero acceleration.
question.explanation: False. The planet's direction changes continuously, so its velocity changes, and a changing velocity is an acceleration. The acceleration is towards the Sun and is caused by gravity.

question.text:
The Sun is a main sequence star. In about 5 billion years it will leave the main sequence.

(a) Describe how the Sun formed from a nebula. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why the Sun is currently stable. (2 marks)

(c) Describe what will happen to the Sun after it leaves the main sequence. (2 marks)
question.hint: For (c), the Sun is not massive enough to become a supernova.
question.explanation: (a) Gravity pulled the dust and gas of the nebula together; as it collapsed it heated up to form a protostar, and when the core was hot enough fusion of hydrogen began. (b) The inward force of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure from the energy released by fusion. (c) The Sun will expand and cool to become a red giant, then its outer layers will be lost and the core will remain as a white dwarf, which eventually cools to a black dwarf.

markScheme.criterion: Gravity pulled the dust and gas together / cloud collapsed under gravity
Temperature increased until fusion of hydrogen started (protostar becomes main sequence)
Gravity acts inwards / tries to collapse the star
Balanced by outward pressure / energy from fusion
Then a white dwarf (and eventually a black dwarf)

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- The **solar system** = the Sun plus planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets, all held by gravity. The Sun is one star in the **Milky Way**, one galaxy in the Universe.
- Stars form when **gravity** collapses a **nebula** into a **protostar**; **fusion** of hydrogen into helium begins and the star joins the **main sequence**, stable because gravity balances the outward pressure from fusion.
- **Sun-sized stars**: red giant → white dwarf → black dwarf. **Massive stars**: red super giant → **supernova** → neutron star or black hole.
- Fusion makes elements up to iron; **supernovae** make heavier elements and scatter them all through space.
- (Higher) In a circular orbit **gravity** provides the force; the object accelerates because its **direction** changes. A **smaller radius needs a higher speed**; change the speed and the radius must change.
- **Natural satellites** are moons; **artificial satellites** are built and launched by people.

practiceQuestions.text: What is the name of the galaxy that contains our solar system?
practiceQuestions.hint: You can see it as a faint band across a dark sky.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Sun and its solar system are part of the Milky Way galaxy.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each object to its description.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what each object orbits and what it is made of.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A moon is a natural satellite of a planet. A comet is icy with a highly elliptical orbit. An asteroid is rocky, mostly found between Mars and Jupiter. A dwarf planet is round but has not cleared its orbit.

pairs.right: A natural satellite orbiting a planet
An icy body with a highly elliptical orbit around the Sun
A rocky body, mostly found between Mars and Jupiter
A round body orbiting the Sun that has not cleared its orbit

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: the Sun produces its energy by burning hydrogen gas.
practiceQuestions.hint: Burning is a chemical reaction. What happens in the Sun's core is nuclear.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. The Sun's energy comes from nuclear fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium, not from burning (combustion).

metadata.blanksText: A star begins as a cloud of dust and gas called a ___, which is pulled together by gravity to form a ___ before fusion begins.

practiceQuestions.text: Which stage in the life cycle of a massive star produces elements heavier than iron?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Elements heavier than iron are formed during a supernova explosion, which also scatters them through space.

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO of these are possible final stages for a star much more massive than the Sun?
practiceQuestions.hint: After the supernova, what is left?
practiceQuestions.explanation: After a supernova the core becomes a neutron star or, for the most massive stars, a black hole. White and black dwarfs are the fate of smaller stars.

practiceQuestions.text: What force keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth?
practiceQuestions.hint: It is a non-contact force that acts between any two masses.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Gravity (the gravitational attraction between the Earth and the Moon) provides the force that keeps the Moon in orbit.

practiceQuestions.text: A geostationary satellite completes one orbit of the Earth in 24 hours. Its orbit has a circumference of about 265 000 km. Calculate its average orbital speed in km/h. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
A satellite is in a stable circular orbit around the Earth. Explain why the satellite is accelerating even though its speed is constant, and state what would happen if its speed decreased.
practiceQuestions.hint: Velocity is a vector. Think about direction.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The satellite's direction is constantly changing, so its velocity is changing even though its speed is not; a changing velocity is an acceleration, caused by gravity acting towards the centre of the Earth. If its speed decreased, gravity would pull it into a smaller orbit (lower radius).

markScheme.criterion: Direction is constantly changing so velocity changes (velocity is a vector)
Changing velocity means acceleration, caused by gravity towards the centre
If speed decreased the orbit radius would decrease / it would move to a lower orbit

practiceQuestions.text:
The Earth contains large amounts of iron, and small amounts of gold and uranium.

(a) Explain how elements as heavy as iron are formed in stars. (2 marks)

(b) Explain how gold and uranium came to be present in the Earth. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: Iron is the heaviest element made by normal fusion. Anything heavier needs a supernova.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Fusion in the cores of stars joins lighter nuclei to form heavier ones; in massive stars this continues in stages, building elements up to iron. (b) Elements heavier than iron are made in supernova explosions, which scatter the elements into space; the solar system formed from a nebula that included this material from earlier stars.

markScheme.criterion: Nuclear fusion joins lighter nuclei to make heavier nuclei
In massive stars fusion continues through stages up to iron
Elements heavier than iron are formed in a supernova
The supernova scattered the elements into space and the solar system formed from this material
